newsitem.title: UK: EBRD stirs nuclear storm with Ukraine review.
newsitem.headline: EBRD stirs nuclear storm with Ukraine review.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's independent panel to study the completion of two nuclear reactors to replace Chernobyl will not have enough time to perform a thorough review, say insiders.
The panel will examine the feasibility of getting the Khmelnitsky 2 and Rivne 4 nuclear reactors up and running in time for the closure of Chernobyl by the year 2000.

"Given the sensitivity of issues concerning nuclear power in Ukraine, it is of the utmost importance that the economic due diligence for financing the completion of K2/R4 is carried out by an independent authority," the London-based development bank said in a statement.

However, sources close to the study said the timescale for completion by November 29 was simply too tight to give the panel, which will be led by British academic John Surrey, a realistic chance of looking at alternatives to nuclear power.
"I do not think too many of the lenders were happy with his appointment as head of the panel," said one.
Environmental organsations say that the bank's role in nuclear financing has always been controversial, but gave a guarded welcome to the appointment of Professor Surrey.

"He is not known as being pro-alternative energy but is independent enough to give a fairly tough decision. It just seems a shame that having appointed a panel, they are giving them so little time. It needs a year at least," said Jon Hontelez of Friends of the Earth International.

Insiders at the EBRD say that work on some areas of the bank's due diligence process has already started and that the independent panel will not be able to spend much time on the ground in Ukraine and will base a large part of its findings on an existing report which is already regarded as heavily flawed.
"It is extremely important to get Chernobyl closed and we have to ask whether there is any way that we get the Ukraine to agree to this without these plants," said one.

The EBRD has frequently been criticised for what environmental campaigners describe as its "pro-nuclear" stance and Austria threatened to withdraw from the EBRD over potential financing for a nuclear reactor in Mohovce, Slovakia.
The bank's 1996 annual meeting in Bulgaria was disrupted by anti-nuclear activists, who distributed imitation dollar bills emblazoned with the EBRD's logo and "In Nuke We Trust".

Campaigners note that the EBRD, which was set up to aid the transition of centrally planned economies in central and eastern Europe to market economies, still finances nuclear programmes, whereas the World Bank will have nothing to do with nuclear.
"The EBRD president is a Frenchman, and its major backers in Britain, Germany and France are all keen to secure contracts for their nuclear industry," said Hontelez of Friends of the Earth.
Greenpeace believes Ukraine, which is one of the least efficient energy users in the world and spends two-thirds of export revenues on energy imports, has massive potential for wind power.

"We are sure when the panel reports, they will find that nuclear is not the least cost option if they take into account waste, decommissioning and the huge potential savings from energy efficiency and use of renewable energy," said Karen Richardson, a nuclear campaigner for Greepeace International.
Others commentators note that the sheer complexity of installing two 1,000 megawatt nuclear and matching demand to supply is fraught with danger.
"There really is total ignorance of what can be done on the demand side of this equation as well as the longer term costs," said an industry specialist.

Under the terms of a memorandum of understanding signed by the Group of Seven industrialised nations and Ukraine in 1995, detailed engineering and procurement work has to start on the two reactors by mid-1997 in order for them to be connected to the Ukraine's power grid by the year 2000.
